title: Jury to hear circumstances of fatal pepper-spray incident
article: An inquest began Monday into Vernon Dale Crowe's death inside an ambulance on July 10, 2001.

In his opening remarks, coroner Hugh Harradence told the six jurors they'll hear how Crowe became "aggressive" following a seizure at a downtown soup kitchen. Crowe head-butted and tried to bite a Regina Police Service constable, and the officer pepper- sprayed him inside an ambulance, Harradence said.
Shortly after, "there was a medical concern (for Crowe)," he said. An hour after the ambulance was called, Crowe was pronounced dead.
A pathologist will tell the jury Crowe didn't die from injuries or a heart attack, but from "excited delirium," Harradence said, providing no further details.

Lawyer Darren Winegarden, who represents the Crowe family, told reporters the Crowes want answers. "They have a lot of concerns about the way things unfolded on that day," he said, admitting pepper spray is among those concerns.
Souls Harbour Mission founder Geri Carroll described Crowe as a "happy-go-lucky" fellow who not only ate at the mission, but volunteered there over the past 11 years.
"I've never known him to be violent," she testified.
Vonda Knipfel said Crowe, her cousin, suffered severe seizures every couple weeks. "They were very violent seizures. He would clench up and convulse on the floor," she said.
If she saw him seizing, Knipfel would place him on his side and keep him safe until it passed. Afterwards, he would fall asleep for 10 to 20 minutes, then get up and appear unsteady.
"I don't think he was ever aggressive after a seizure. He was confused," she said.

She recalled once seeing Crowe resisting paramedics' attempts to take him to the hospital. "He would just want to go home," she said, adding the after-effects of his seizure were often confused for drunkenness.

When Crowe suffered a seizure inside Souls Harbour Mission on July 10, 2001, volunteers placed him on his side and called an ambulance. But before paramedics arrived, Crowe regained consciousness. He told Carroll he was OK, but she suggested he get checked out anyway. He replied, "If you say so," said Carroll, who became emotional.

From his chair at the mission, Darryl Gregorash watched through a window as Crowe calmly walked with paramedics to the ambulance. At one point, a paramedic exited the ambulance, went inside the cab, then returned to the back of the ambulance. Within minutes, a police officer arrived, Gregorash said.
He said the police officer opened the ambulance's side door and stepped up. Gregorash saw the officer reach for something shiny -- which he took for handcuffs.
"I was certain he was trying to handcuff him," he said. The officer quickly stepped back. "He lurched back, as if he'd been hit," Gregorash said. He was emphatic that he never saw any pepper spray.
When Gregorash stepped outside moments later, a paramedic was doing chest compressions on Crowe.

The jury, which was deliberately made up of three aboriginal jurors and three non-aboriginal, is expected to hear from 21 witnesses over the next five to seven days. Crowe was aboriginal and his death has drawn criticism from the Saskatchewan Coalition Against Racism.
